question: Can a transformer trained on simulated parameter-and-sample pairs serve as a one-pass point estimator for univariate distribution parameters and achieve lower integrated mean-squared error than clipped maximum-likelihood or method-of-moments estimators?

key_findings.claim: Under fixed, known parameter ranges, the trained transformer has lower reported mean-squared error than the paper's range-clipped maximum-likelihood baseline for every tested Exponential and Normal sample-size setting.
key_findings.evidence: For Exponential scale beta drawn uniformly from [0.5,2], Table 2 reports transformer versus clipped-MLE MSE of 0.0796 versus 0.1113 at n=10, 0.0375 versus 0.0445 at n=30, 0.0143 versus 0.0149 at n=100, and 0.0413 versus 0.0503 for log-uniform n in [10,100]. For Normal mu drawn from [-5,5] and sigma from [1,10], Table 4 reports 1.7337 versus 2.2809, 0.7169 versus 0.8056, 0.2492 versus 0.2558, and 0.8106 versus 0.9636 in the same four settings. The largest gains occur at n=10 and shrink with sample size.

anchors.section: Figure 3(a) and Section 4.2.1 Known Parameter Range

key_findings.claim: When the sample is normalized by its observed extrema and the parameter range is described as unknown, the reported results show no consistent transformer advantage.
key_findings.evidence: In Exponential Table 3, the transformer improves MSE at n=10 (0.1613 versus 0.1750) and mixed n (0.0691 versus 0.0730), is indistinguishable at n=30 (0.0584 versus 0.0586, p=0.6673), and is worse at n=100 (0.0182 versus 0.0174). For Normal Table 5, the prose says performance is similar at n=10, n=30, and mixed n and worse at n=100; the first, second, and mixed rows indeed have p=0.5096, 0.1882, and 0.5076. The Normal n=100 numeric model entry is internally corrupted and is not treated as evidence.

anchors.section: Section 4.2.2 Unknown Parameter Range and Table 3

key_findings.claim: The central experiment is more accurately interpreted as learning a prior-dependent Bayes point estimator than as replacing statistical derivation with a distribution-free estimator.
key_findings.evidence: Each training example first draws parameters from specified uniform ranges, then draws a sample conditional on those parameters, and the model minimizes squared parameter error over 9.9 million such pairs. The population minimizer of squared loss is the conditional mean of the parameter under that joint training distribution. The known-range model therefore receives the same bounded prior support used to generate the tests, while the 'unknown-range' model still trains and tests under the fixed beta, mu, and sigma ranges even though per-sample scale is hidden from the transformer input.

anchors.section: Section 1 Introduction, training construction and MSE objective

key_findings.claim: The Normal unknown-range n=100 result in Table 5 is a demonstrable transcription or calculation error and cannot support a quantitative comparison.
key_findings.evidence: Table 5 prints transformer mean/std 0.0182/0.0323, exactly duplicating the Exponential unknown-range transformer n=100 entry in Table 3. If 0.0182 were compared with the printed Normal MLE mean 0.2780, the transformer would be dramatically better, but the surrounding prose says it is worse and the reported t-value is negative (-2.7978, p=0.0051), which also indicates the authors intended the opposite ordering under their sign convention. All three elements cannot be true simultaneously.

key_findings.claim: The Beta experiment does not substantiate the abstract's claim of a maximum-likelihood comparison because the baseline's identity and implementation are inconsistent and unauditable.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.4 says numerical Beta MLE is unavailable in open source and explicitly chooses method of moments for 0<alpha,beta<1; the prose after Table 6 again calls the comparison method of moments. Table 6 instead labels the baseline 'MLE'. Its baseline MSE also rises from 0.0933 at n=10 to 0.3313 at n=30 and remains 0.2873 at n=100, behavior that is suspicious for a consistently implemented moments estimator, while no code or formula is supplied. Table 7 extends the transformer to 0.5<alpha,beta<5 but gives no competing estimator at all.

key_findings.claim: The experiment inventory is internally inconsistent: the settings promise a Poisson study, but the paper reports Beta instead and contains no Poisson method or result.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.1 lists Normal, Exponential, and Poisson as the three tested distributions. The actual subsections and Tables 2-7 cover Exponential, Normal, and Beta, matching the abstract; Poisson never reappears. This appears to be an uncorrected experiment-description error rather than evidence for a fourth family.

key_findings.claim: The proposed input is an order-invariant, softly binned empirical distribution encoded as a long transformer sequence, not a sequence of observations in their original order.
key_findings.evidence: After mapping sample values to [0,1], Seq-first divides the range into L=1024 position bins and each position into K=384 sub-bins; each observation contributes linearly interpolated weight to two adjacent dimensions. Contributions from repeated observations are accumulated in the same bins, so permuting observations leaves the input unchanged. The alternative Embed-first layout performs poorly on the Normal n=30 ablation (MSE 3.155), whereas Seq-first with the shortened RoBERTa reaches 0.7169 and the original RoBERTa reaches 0.7215.

key_findings.claim: The amortization argument is incomplete because the paper reports substantial per-setting simulation and training cost but no inference latency, model-count accounting, or break-even analysis.
key_findings.evidence: The reported default is 9.9 million generated training examples and 100,000 test examples for each setting on an A6000 GPU. Table 1 gives 63 h 35 min for the selected six-layer, 384-dimensional, length-1024 model and 91 h 43 min for standard RoBERTa in one Normal n=30 setting. The text calls 60-70 GPU hours negligible and says training is needed once per distribution, yet the evaluation varies range handling and fixed versus mixed sample sizes and does not say which settings share a model. No one-pass latency, simulator cost, memory, energy, repeated-query volume, or optimized classical-runtime comparison is reported.

key_findings.claim: The reported p-values overstate the diagnostic value of small risk differences because corresponding estimators are evaluated on the same simulated cases but the paper uses unpaired two-sample tests over 100,000 errors.
key_findings.evidence: Every result table labels its statistic a two-sample t-test even though MLE and transformer errors can be paired by generated test sample. With 100,000 cases, the known-range Normal n=100 difference is only 0.0066 MSE (0.2492 versus 0.2558) and the known-range Exponential n=100 difference is 0.0006 (0.0143 versus 0.0149), yet both are reported as p=0.0001. No confidence interval, paired effect estimate, seed-level replication, or correction across settings is provided.

key_findings.claim: The empirical evidence is limited to family-specific interpolation of point estimates and does not validate uncertainty, likelihood-free generalization to a new simulator, or parameters outside the training support.
key_findings.evidence: A separate model and simulator-generated training distribution are introduced for each named family. All tests use the same parameter ranges and sampling mechanisms as training; 'unknown range' only changes the normalization visible to the network. Outputs are single parameter vectors, with no posterior, interval coverage, calibration, held-out family, misspecified distribution, contaminated sample, multivariate case, or out-of-range parameter evaluation. The paper itself restricts the study to univariate distributions.

method.core_idea: Amortize parameter estimation by repeatedly simulating a parameter from a chosen training range and an i.i.d. sample from the corresponding univariate distribution, then train a transformer regressor to minimize parameter mean-squared error.
method.mechanism: Values are clipped or normalized into [0,1] and accumulated into a sparse soft histogram represented by 1024 transformer positions with 384 dimensions each. Seq-first assigns an observation to a position interval and linearly splits its mass between neighboring embedding dimensions. A RoBERTa-derived encoder, shortened from 12 layers at width 768 to six layers at width 384 to accommodate length 1024, maps the fixed representation to its first final-layer output; a fully connected head predicts one or two parameters. Known-range experiments use fixed normalization and bounded outputs. Unknown-range experiments divide by the sample maximum for Exponential data or min-max normalize Normal data, then externally rescale predicted normalized parameters by the observed extrema before computing squared loss.
assumptions: The distribution family is known and a simulator can cheaply draw both parameters and observations even when the analytic density is unavailable.
Uniform training ranges over beta, mu, sigma, alpha, and beta encode an appropriate prior and match deployment well enough for integrated training risk to be relevant.
A point estimate under squared loss is sufficient; posterior shape, uncertainty, identifiability, and interval coverage are not required.
Clipping samples and estimates to the chosen bounds does not create an unfair information asymmetry or material tail bias.
A 1024-by-384 soft-binned empirical distribution preserves the sample information needed for all tested parameter values.
Training and test simulations from the same parameter ranges, family, and numerical generator measure the desired generalization rather than interpolation under a fixed prior predictive distribution.
Observed sample extrema provide stable scale recovery for the unknown-range transformations, including at small n.
The transformer architecture is responsible for the gain beyond the prior, bounded loss, discretization, and shrinkage available to simpler estimators.
Nine-point-nine million on-the-fly simulations per setting are available and 60-70 A6000 GPU hours can be amortized over enough downstream estimates.
Mean-squared error averaged across parameters is an appropriate common objective even when parameters have different scales.

techniques.role: Creates supervised parameter-and-sample pairs without evaluating a likelihood or deriving an estimator.
Maps each normalized scalar observation to adjacent high-resolution bins with linear interpolation and aggregates the unordered sample.
Converts fixed bounded inputs or per-sample extrema into a [0,1] representation before regression.
Uses a RoBERTa-derived attention stack and a fully connected head to map an empirical distribution representation to one or two parameters.
Pays simulation and training cost once for a fixed setting so each later parameter estimate is a forward pass.
Restores the output scale from a sample maximum or min-max interval when explicit ranges are hidden from the transformer.
Clips known-range MLE outputs to the same declared parameter support used for training and testing.
Estimates integrated parameter MSE on 100,000 fresh simulations for fixed and variable sample sizes.

evaluations.setting: Normal parameters mu~Uniform[-5,5], sigma~Uniform[1,10], sample size 30, known range, 9.9M training and 100K test examples
evaluations.metric: Mean parameter MSE and wall-clock training time
evaluations.result: Standard RoBERTa reaches 0.7215 in 91 h 43 min; the six-layer width-384 length-1024 Seq-first model reaches 0.7169 in 63 h 35 min; Embed-first reaches 3.155 in 63 h 24 min
evaluations.baseline: Range-clipped Normal MLE at 0.8056 MSE, plus standard RoBERTa and the alternative Embed-first representation

evaluations.setting: Exponential beta~Uniform[0.5,2] with known range; fixed n=10, 30, 100 and log-uniform n in [10,100]
evaluations.metric: Mean/std of per-case squared parameter error over 100K tests
evaluations.result: Transformer mean MSE is 0.0796, 0.0375, 0.0143, and 0.0413 across the four settings
evaluations.baseline: Sample-mean MLE clipped to [0.5,2], with MSE 0.1113, 0.0445, 0.0149, and 0.0503

evaluations.setting: Exponential beta~Uniform[0.5,2] with per-sample maximum normalization described as unknown range
evaluations.metric: Mean/std squared parameter error and reported two-sample t-test over 100K tests
evaluations.result: Transformer versus MLE MSE is 0.1613 versus 0.1750 at n=10, 0.0584 versus 0.0586 at n=30, 0.0182 versus 0.0174 at n=100, and 0.0691 versus 0.0730 for mixed n; the n=30 difference is nonsignificant and the n=100 result favors MLE

evaluations.setting: Normal mu~Uniform[-5,5], sigma~Uniform[1,10] with known range; fixed n=10, 30, 100 and log-uniform n in [10,100]
evaluations.metric: Mean/std of MSE averaged over mu and sigma over 100K tests
evaluations.result: Transformer mean MSE is 1.7337, 0.7169, 0.2492, and 0.8106 across the four settings
evaluations.baseline: Normal MLE with mu and sigma clipped to their generation ranges, with MSE 2.2809, 0.8056, 0.2558, and 0.9636

evaluations.setting: Normal parameters with per-sample min-max normalization described as unknown range
evaluations.metric: Mean/std parameter MSE and reported two-sample t-test over 100K tests
evaluations.result: The valid rows show transformer versus MLE MSE of 2.8768 versus 2.8637 at n=10, 0.9402 versus 0.9316 at n=30, and 1.1376 versus 1.1309 for mixed n, all nonsignificant; the n=100 transformer number is excluded because it is internally corrupted
evaluations.baseline: Unclipped Normal sample mean and population-denominator sample standard deviation

evaluations.setting: Beta parameters 0<alpha,beta<1 and 0.5<alpha,beta<5; fixed and mixed sample sizes
evaluations.result: For 0<alpha,beta<1, Table 6 reports transformer MSE 0.0235, 0.0123, 0.0054, and 0.0131 versus a baseline of 0.0933, 0.3313, 0.2873, and 0.1756; for 0.5<alpha,beta<5, transformer-only MSE is 0.543, 0.287, 0.122, and 0.302
evaluations.baseline: An unauditable baseline called method of moments in Section 4.4 and prose but MLE in Table 6; Table 7 has no baseline

limitations: The simulation prior and test parameter distribution are the same, so lower integrated MSE does not establish robustness to a different parameter population.

The MSE-trained network is compared with MLE rather than the matched posterior-mean Bayes estimator, MAP, analytic shrinkage, bias-corrected estimators, or an equivalently prior-aware classical decision rule.
Only three univariate families are actually evaluated; no multivariate, high-dimensional, discrete, mixture, censored, dependent, or simulator-only application is tested.
The claim that a density is unnecessary is not tested on an unknown-density simulator; every experiment uses a standard analytic distribution with cheap estimators.
No posterior samples, confidence or credible intervals, calibration, coverage, or decision-sensitive uncertainty metric is produced.
No parameter value outside the fixed training support, held-out subrange, shifted prior, misspecified family, contamination, outlier, or numerical-generator change is evaluated.
The 'unknown parameter range' condition still trains and tests under fixed parameter ranges and uses observed extrema outside the transformer to restore scale.
The Normal n=100 unknown-range result is corrupted by an apparent copy from the Exponential table and contradicts its prose and t-statistic.
The Beta baseline is called method of moments in prose and MLE in the table, has suspicious sample-size behavior, and has no disclosed formula or implementation.
The settings section promises Poisson experiments, but no Poisson experiment exists.

The paper reports no code, random seeds, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, checkpoint rule, model initialization details, or exact mapping from experimental settings to separately trained models.
The arXiv record and paper link no code, data, trained weights, supplement, or reproducibility artifact; an exact-title GitHub repository search also returned no repository as of the review date.
The two-sample t-tests ignore the natural pairing of estimator errors on the same test draws and provide no seed-level or confidence-interval analysis.
Tiny absolute gains become highly significant at 100,000 test cases, while practical effect sizes and amortization break-even are not analyzed.

The high-resolution representation and self-attention are expensive relative to sufficient statistics or direct set encoders, and no small MLP, histogram network, DeepSets, or Set Transformer ablation isolates the role of the transformer.
Input clipping discards tails in known-range experiments and may inject bias that differs across the learned estimator and the baseline.
The conclusion asserts that real-world parameter ranges are usually known without evidence or evaluation.
The claim that 60-70 GPU hours are negligible compares compute with human derivation but omits mature statistical libraries, simulation cost, inference latency, energy, and query-volume break-even.
failure_modes: A deployment prior differs from the uniform training prior, turning learned shrinkage toward the training support into systematic bias.
A true parameter lies outside the training range, causing bounded outputs or learned interpolation to saturate rather than extrapolate.
The assumed family is misspecified, so a family-specific model returns a confident-looking point estimate with no goodness-of-fit warning.
Outliers or heavy tails are clipped into boundary bins and become indistinguishable, corrupting scale estimates.
At small n, the maximum or min-max interval is unstable and makes unknown-range rescaling noisy; at large n, MLE becomes efficient and the learned shrinkage advantage vanishes or reverses.
The soft histogram aliases observations that fall into the same bins and loses information required by a more complex or multivariate family.
A change in sample-size distribution alters aggregate bin mass and moves the input outside the lengths seen in training.
Simulation mismatch, numerical precision changes, censoring, dependence, or measurement noise creates samples absent from the prior predictive training distribution.
Training a separate large model for every family, range regime, and sample-size policy costs more than direct optimization before enough repeated queries arrive.
A point estimate hides multimodality or weak identification, yielding a plausible mean in a low-posterior-density region.
Table or implementation errors go undetected because neither code nor exact baseline definitions are available for reproduction.
reusable_insights: Simulation-trained squared-loss regression is a practical way to approximate a posterior mean when a simulator and an explicit deployment prior are available but a tractable likelihood is not.
State the training parameter distribution as a prior and compare against Bayes-risk-matched baselines; otherwise a neural estimator's shrinkage gain can be misattributed to architecture.
An unordered scalar sample can be encoded as an interpolated empirical histogram, preserving permutation invariance while giving a neural model a fixed-size input.
Normalize parameters and observations carefully, but distinguish a model that is scale-equivariant from one that merely trains on a fixed hidden scale range.
Report both integrated risk under the training prior and conditional risk across parameter bins so improvements are not driven by high-density interior regions.
Pair errors by simulated dataset and report confidence intervals and effect sizes, not only p-values from large synthetic test sets.

Include posterior mean, MAP, MLE, bias-corrected, shrinkage, DeepSets, Set Transformer, and neural posterior-estimation baselines to isolate objective, prior, representation, and architecture effects.
Test shifted priors, held-out parameter intervals, contamination, family misspecification, and simulator changes before presenting amortized inference as broadly reusable.
Measure simulation throughput, training cost, inference latency, memory, and the query count where amortization beats a mature classical implementation.
Audit every quantitative table against prose, signs, and duplicated values before using it as evidence; internally contradictory rows should be quarantined rather than silently averaged.
open_questions: How close is the transformer to the exact posterior mean under the paper's uniform priors for Normal, Exponential, and Beta families?
Do the apparent MSE gains remain after comparison with analytic or numerical posterior means and simple prior-aware shrinkage estimators?
Can the method retain calibration and accuracy under shifted parameter priors, out-of-range parameters, contaminated observations, and misspecified families?
Does a DeepSets or Set Transformer encoder operating directly on observations match the result with less memory and without a 393,216-cell bin grid?
What exact Beta estimator generated Table 6, and why does its error increase sharply from n=10 to n=30?
What is the correct Normal unknown-range n=100 transformer result, and can all tables be reproduced from released seeds and code?
How many distinct models were trained across family, range, and sample-size settings, and what is the actual amortization break-even against SciPy or other optimized estimators?
Can one conditional model handle multiple families and return both a goodness-of-fit signal and a full posterior rather than a family-specific point estimate?
How does discretization resolution affect bias, tail sensitivity, sample-size generalization, and compute?
Would training on a hierarchy of priors or using empirical-Bayes adaptation improve performance when the deployment parameter distribution is unknown?
Can the approach handle multivariate observations, dependence, missingness, censoring, and non-identifiable parameters while preserving permutation symmetries?
Which result was intended by the Poisson statement: an omitted experiment, or a stale description that should have named Beta?

competitive_landscape.title: Likelihood-Free Parameter Estimation with Neural Bayes Estimators
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct prior that already formulates simulator-trained neural point estimation as amortized, likelihood-free Bayes estimation.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sainsbury-Dale et al. explicitly connect the training loss and parameter prior to Bayes-optimal point estimators, use permutation-invariant networks for replicated data, provide open-source software, bootstrap uncertainty, extensive simulations, and a real spatial-extremes application. The reviewed paper applies a RoBERTa-derived model and a new soft-bin encoding to elementary univariate families but omits the Bayes framing and uncertainty.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers Can Do Bayesian Inference
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior transformer approach trained on prior-sampled synthetic tasks for single-forward-pass Bayesian inference.
competitive_landscape.difference: Muller et al.'s Prior-Data Fitted Networks approximate predictive posteriors for new supervised tasks and demonstrate broad Gaussian-process, Bayesian-neural-network, tabular, and image settings with released code. The reviewed paper instead regresses distribution parameters from a binned scalar sample and returns only a point estimate, but its uniform simulation training follows the same prior-fitted logic.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards a Neural Statistician
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational prior for learning permutation-invariant dataset-level statistics with neural networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: Edwards and Storkey learn unsupervised latent statistics that summarize entire datasets for clustering, transfer, representative selection, and unseen-class classification. The reviewed paper supervises explicit distribution parameters and uses a discretized empirical distribution rather than a hierarchical variational set model.

competitive_landscape.title: Set Transformer: A Framework for Attention-based Permutation-Invariant Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct architecture alternative for attention over unordered samples.
competitive_landscape.difference: Lee et al. build permutation invariance into attention over set elements and introduce inducing-point attention with linear rather than quadratic complexity in set size. The reviewed paper first aggregates observations into 1024 ordered value bins and runs a generic RoBERTa stack, without comparing against a principled set encoder.

competitive_landscape.title: Automatic Posterior Transformation for Likelihood-Free Inference
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior simulation-based inference competitor that learns a full posterior when the likelihood is unavailable.
competitive_landscape.difference: Greenberg et al.'s sequential neural posterior estimation supports arbitrary adaptive proposal distributions and flow-based conditional densities and operates on high-dimensional time series and images. The reviewed method uses many prior simulations once and returns a point estimate for small scalar samples, with no posterior or adaptive simulation allocation.

competitive_landscape.title: All-in-one simulation-based inference
competitive_landscape.relationship: Near-concurrent broader amortized transformer competitor for simulation-based Bayesian inference.
competitive_landscape.difference: Gloeckler et al.'s Simformer trains a transformer diffusion model over the joint parameter-data space, samples arbitrary conditionals including posterior and likelihood, and handles missing or unstructured observations and function-valued parameters in ecology, epidemiology, and neuroscience. The reviewed paper predicts only fixed-family scalar point parameters from complete univariate samples.

competitive_landscape.title: Can Transformers Learn Full Bayesian Inference in Context?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later extension of prior-fitted transformers from point or predictive outputs to full posterior inference.
competitive_landscape.difference: Reuter et al. combine prior-fitted networks with continuous normalizing flows to draw posterior samples for generalized linear and latent-factor models and compare them with MCMC and variational inference on real data. The reviewed paper has no posterior representation, real dataset, or strong Bayesian baseline.

competitive_landscape.title: Universal priors: solving empirical Bayes via Bayesian inference and pretraining
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later theory that directly analyzes why a synthetically pretrained Bayes estimator can adapt beyond its training distribution.
competitive_landscape.difference: Cannella et al. identify universal training priors and prove near-optimal empirical-Bayes regret for Poisson problems, explaining distribution adaptation and length generalization through posterior contraction. The reviewed paper supplies neither an empirical-Bayes adaptation mechanism nor theory and, despite naming Poisson in its settings, reports no Poisson experiment.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a novel transformer approach that estimates distribution parameters without a closed-form estimator, mathematical derivation, or even a known probability density, using a precise sample-to-embedding conversion and one forward pass after training.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Pages 1-3 state the novelty and advantages; pages 4-6 define range normalization, the Seq-first and Embed-first representations, and transformer regression; pages 7-12 report the synthetic comparisons and conclude that the method is an ideal estimator, especially when parameter ranges are known.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The broad contribution is not novel: before this submission, neural Bayes estimators already mapped replicated simulator data to likelihood-free amortized point estimates, explicitly derived their Bayes-optimal relationship to the prior and loss, used permutation-invariant networks, released software, quantified uncertainty, and demonstrated a real application. Prior-Data Fitted Networks had also established transformers trained on prior-sampled synthetic tasks for single-forward Bayesian inference, while Set Transformer and neural posterior-estimation work supplied stronger architectures and full-distribution alternatives. The narrow residual contribution is the particular Seq-first soft histogram fed to a shortened RoBERTa model and a small synthetic comparison on Normal, Exponential, and Beta parameters. Even that evidence is weakened by an unmatched prior-free MLE baseline, no simpler set/histogram ablation, a corrupted Normal row, an unidentified Beta baseline, and an absent promised Poisson experiment. Later Simformer, full-Bayesian ICL, and universal-prior theory further subsume the claimed breadth.

reviewer_notes: The extracted text was read end to end and matched the pinned 12-page PDF. Every PDF page was rendered and visually inspected at full resolution, including equations (1)-(3), Figures 1-4, Tables 1-7, plot axes and legends, architecture and encoding diagrams, footnote, and references. The PDF and extracted-text SHA-256 values were independently recomputed and match the full-text index. The Normal Table 5 n=100 transformer entry 0.0182/0.0323 exactly duplicates Exponential Table 3 and contradicts both the Normal prose and t-statistic, so it is documented but excluded from evaluation evidence. The Beta baseline label conflict and missing Poisson experiment were likewise confirmed visually. ArXiv v1 contains no comment or artifact link, the paper references no implementation, and an exact-title GitHub repository search returned zero repositories; there was therefore no external code or supplement to inspect. Competitor research was checked through 2026-08-23 using primary arXiv or official PMLR records across four focused families: neural Bayes point estimation, prior-fitted transformer inference, permutation-invariant set estimators, and simulation-based full-posterior inference plus later empirical-Bayes theory.
